candidates.review_note: Let k=n/2. Losing positions are exactly those where the minimum pile size occurs more than k times. From such a nonterminal position every move must touch a minimum pile; the new smaller minimum can occur only among the k changed piles, so the result is winning. From any other position, at least k piles exceed the minimum; reduce exactly k of them to that minimum, creating a losing position. When the minimum is zero and occurs more than k times, fewer than k nonempty piles remain and no move exists. This proves the criterion by induction on the total stones.

Squaring an odd-length permutation cycle preserves one cycle of that length, while squaring an even-length cycle produces two cycles of half its length. Consequently every even cycle length in the target permutation must occur an even number of times. This is also sufficient: take an internal square root for each odd cycle and interleave each pair of equal even cycles into one twice-long cycle. Count cycles, including fixed points, and check exactly this parity condition.
